Resistance of some Clostridium spp. to penicillin and clindamycin had declined, but no changes were noted for Cl. perfringens. The emergence of multi-drug resistant anaerobes has been noted.5 The B. fragilis group are the most frequently isolated anaerobic bacteria in clinical infections and all members of the group may be pathogenic.6 Most strains produce beta lactamase and thus are resistant to penicillins and cepha- losporins although there is varied susceptibility within the group.7 In a survey of susceptibility patterns8 the most ac- tive drugs in vitro against B. fragilis group strains were im- ipenem, metronidazole, and chloramphenicol; resistance to cefoxitin, clindamycin, and piperacillin was not wide- spread and combinations of beta-lactamase inhibitors with penicillins or cephalosporins (e.g. ampicillin or cefopera- zone with sulbactam; ticarcillin with clavulanate) were also very active. Others have reported similar results.7 On the basis of activity in vitro in another study9 metronida- zole, imipenem, ticarcillin with clavulanate, cefoxitin, and amoxicillin with clavulanate were considered suitable for the treatment of B. fragilis group infections. However, a more recent commentary5 suggested that cefoxitin and clindamycin were no longer drugs of choice due to in- creasing resistance. A clinical isolate of B. fragilis, simul- taneously resistant to metronidazole, amoxicillin with cla- vulanate, and imipenem, was reported in the UK;10 treatment with clindamycin was successful on this occa- sion. Tigecycline is considered promising for the manage- ment of anaerobic infections; other drugs with potential for oral therapy may include nitazoxanide, ramoplanin, and ri- faximin.5 1.
